name: +24% of GMV, Hiding across funnel steps
summary: We were watching one funnel. There were six, and they disagreed with each other. The aggregate rate was the average of a business that worked and a business that didn't, and averaging them hid the fact that the fix needed nothing built.

items: Tore down 3 quarters of the booking funnel, every confirmed order, matched to the catalogue with no unresolved rows, across every live partner instance, segmented on tier × destination.
+24% of annual GMV found recoverable, sitting in 3 live steps; no new product, supplier, or renegotiated deal.
Impact area: Revenue, by finding it rather than building anything.
Hero: the business, choosing where next quarter's build capacity goes.
The shape of the problem: searches/day ×3.9, conversion ×0.78 over the same three quarters. We bought 3.9× the traffic and got 2.7× the money.
Blind spot: one conversion rate for every tier, every destination, every price point, six quite different businesses reported as one.
Pain: no way to tell whether the product got worse or the mix moved. Those have opposite roadmaps.
Stakes: the build plan was about to absorb a quarter, when the loss might already be sitting in screens shipped months ago.
My hypothesis: the aggregate is the average of segments that behave nothing alike, and the averaging is what hides the answer.
SMART objective: explain the decline by segment and size what is recoverable, within one quarter.
North Star: recoverable GMV as a share of run rate, actionable, not diagnostic.
Primary: step conversion by segment, order value by segment, take rate by price band.
Secondary: segment GMV share, quarter-on-quarter share movement.
Owned: the question, the data model, the grain, the method, the sizing, the recommendation.
The grain decision: built the segment funnel at session × property, because tier only exists on one event in the chain, end-to-end session grain would have thrown it away.

Rebuilt the base, didn't caveat it: the dimension every report leaned on was wrong. Reconstructed it from confirmed orders, with every booked property matched to the catalogue, no unresolved rows, no silent exclusions.
Segmented on what changes behaviour: tier × destination segments; then order size, and partner across every live instance.

Step by step, not end to end: end-to-end says a segment is worse; steps say where. Each finding was one step, a segment beating its counterpart at every step, then converting at less than half at exactly one.
Held the property constant: compared partners only on properties booked through both, so inventory stopped being the variable and the only difference left was what the guest was shown.

Tested what everyone knew: bucketed every click by price position against the rest of that page, bands, cheapest to 2.5× page average. Conversion is flat across all. At the premium tier it inverts: the cheapest rooms convert at about half the rate of ones priced just below average.
Ended on decisions, not findings: 4 questions to named owners, each answerable yes or no.
+24% of annual GMV recoverable, across funnel steps screens, none requiring anything built or renegotiated.
The decline explained: conversion fell because the mix moved, not because the product degraded, which changed the question from what's broken to where do we spend.
A pricing assumption retired: being cheapest buys nothing, and at the premium tier it costs. Redirected promotional spend rather than adding to it.
Method reused: segment → step → isolate → size → limit is now how funnel questions get answered here.

name: From Search to Licensed API
summary: Two-thirds of users never touch a sort or a filter, they take the list exactly as we ordered it. So the ranking is not a feature, it is the storefront. This is how we rebuilt it from what people actually type, and how it ended up being sold to other companies.

items: Owned hotel search & discovery e2e, from the question a user is asking to the order they get back.
87.5% of GMV now flows through the default ranking. Same engine licensed externally as an API, another travel business running its entire hotel operation on it.
Impact area: Revenue, via decision quality, not traffic.
Hero: a traveller booking a hotel, high-stakes, infrequent, no way to inspect before paying.
Blind spot: we could see what users chose. We could not see what they were asking for.
Pain: searches returning noise or nothing, the two were indistinguishable in the data, so neither could be fixed.
Stakes: two-thirds of results-page sessions never touch a sort or a filter. The default order isn't a feature, it's the storefront.
Constraints: no data scientist, no ranking infra, shared QA, pod of 8 across two products, weekly release train.
My hypothesis: ranking quality, not filter count, decides GMV, and ranking can't be fixed until the input is understood.
SMART objective: ship a measurable default ranking in a quarter, and prove it beats what users pick for themselves.
North Star: share of GMV flowing through the default order.
Primary KPIs: GMV share, conversion by sort, AOV by sort.
Secondary KPIs: no-result rate, selection depth, sort adoption.
Owned: the full surface, input, relevance, ranking, filters, geo, and the instrumentation under all of it.
Process: JTBD on the query → instrument → measure → spec → ship → re-measure. Nothing shipped on an opinion.
Key players: 1 BE, shared QA.

Closed the instrumentation gap: until we could see what was being asked for, relevance was being scored against clicks the system had produced itself, a closed loop that can only confirm itself. Everything below depends on breaking it.

Made results unambiguous: users could not tell what kind of thing each result referred to. Removing that ambiguity also split two failure modes that had looked identical in the data, and only then could either be fixed.

Treated empty searches as causes, not screens: the instinct is to design a better no-results state. Instead, repeated investigations, each isolating a different failure class. 6 releases in 6 weeks, each off its own research.

Specced the ranking rather than requesting it: chose the signal set and how the signals trade against each other. Most PMs file a ticket for "better ranking", these are product tradeoffs, not engineering ones.
Weights as config, not code: retunable without a release. A modest call at the time; it became the reason the engine was portable, then sellable.
Compared users to themselves: same people's sessions with & without a manual re-sort. Kills the obvious objection, that re-sorters are simply cheaper customers.
Audited the menu on measured performance, not usage: then argued the effort belonged on the default, 1% better first result beats doubling every other option's usage.
Productised it: measurable ordering + config weights = no longer an internal feature. Now licensed as an API.

blocks.text:
Five movements, one story: users find it sooner, engage more often, buy
more often, buy better, and increasingly stop re-ordering the list at
all.

items: Selection depth (average and tail position of the hotel chosen) down ~25%.
Median order value 1.37× over the same window.
1.33× AOV within-user, the default against the same users re-sorted sessions.
The default carries the business, 87.5% of GMV, ~78% of all selections, and two-thirds of users never over-ride with controls.
Licensed externally as an API, other travel business’ running entire hotel operation on it.
Long-term: weights are config → retunable without a release, portable to a new vertical or a new buyer.
Instrument the input before optimising the output: tuning a ranking against its own clicks only ever confirms itself.
The default is the product: two-thirds never touch a control. 1% better first result > doubling every other sort's usage.
Compare people to themselves: turns an interesting correlation into a finding people have to accept.
The denominator changes the answer: one option read well on a loose denominator, badly on a strict one.
Config beats clever: making the weights tunable was a small call that made the engine sellable.

name: Solving Room Mapping and Identity at Scale
summary: String similarity gets the two cases that matter exactly backwards: it merges the rooms that must never merge and splits the ones that must. This is the pipeline we built instead, stage by stage, including the part everyone tries to automate away.

name: Configurator: Visualize, Customize, Compare, Purchase
summary: Dive into hyper-realistic 3D visualization to learn via rotations, cinematics, and features; customize with color/trim swaps, variant comparisons, and accessorize amid interactive doors/lights; then screenshot, save, and purchase direct, turning showroom dreams into ownership seamlessly.

name: Brand-led agent: Expert Guidance, Instant
summary: Hit a snag mid-customization? Summon a live expert via VSA: they grab your screen, guide tweaks with precision, answer queries on the spot, and log sessions for razor-sharp coaching, bridging pixels to perfect purchase decisions.

name: 60% Faster Onboarding, Halved Bounce
summary: Led the redesign of AR scanning and onboarding UX, using funnel diagnostics & user testing to define 3D visual cues, immersive in‑AR onboarding, and gesture refinements.

blocks.text: Re-engineered Royal Enfield AR onboarding (hypothesis-driven, user tested) serving 1.4M users: slashed scan time 60% (<15s), 2x engagement vs brand site (5+ min), halved bounce (↓45 pts), drove 8.6% lead lift.

blocks.caption: New 3D scanning + onboarding flow ⇒ 60% faster via visual guidance + gesture support.

items: User & ICP: Royal Enfield website visitors (Android mobile/tablet, 25-45yo, 2-wheeler buyers) exploring AR visualization before purchase via our first standalone AR deployment.
Core JTBD: "Show me this bike in my garage/space instantly without scanning confusion or tech frustration."
Pain points: >35s median scan time, confusing surface detection, 2D UI onboarding skipped; users needed hand-holding but got static instructions.
Starting hypothesis: "Surface scanning + 2D onboarding friction kills sessions; 3D immersive flows + dynamic visual cues will cut scan time, and bounce."
Success Metrics: Primary: Bounce rate, scan time (<10s). Secondary: Engagement (5+ min), lead conversion.
Scope: Owned scanning + onboarding UX redesign, graphics/visual cues.
Process: Funnel differential analysis → identify bleed → user tests (~30 users) → design → iterate → ship.
Stakeholders: Royal Enfield brand team (approvals), small x-func team (Design/Eng/Graphics), tied to OKRs for module KPIs.
Frameworks: Funnel Diagnostics (bleed localization), JTBD (guided scanning for fast, seamless transition into AR), Usability Testing (contextual tasks + non-leading debriefs).
Discovery: Funnel analysis pinpointed landing → onboarding bleed (>35s scan time); post-onboarding users showed 15-20% leads, 5+ min engagement → isolated scanning as culprit.

Key insight during user-testing: "It would be helpful if I could mark a certain area and the bike would appear there" → birthed "Place Here" feature (visual space preview + placement size and position estimate).
UX overhaul: Redesigned scanning: non-intrusive dynamic 3D visual cues (scannable area feedback, lighting feedback) vs static 2D instructions.
Onboarding pivot: Ditched 2D UI for immersive 3D onboarding integrated into AR experience; taught model interaction via in-world gestures and animations.
Gesture expansion: Supported common variants of user gestures (pinch, drag, rotate) observed in tests and articles; removed uncommon ones causing friction.

Insights and Opportunities: ~30 user tests (recent buyers, first-timers) using contextual tasks ("found this on brand site") + non-leading debriefs surfaced the key pain points and opportunities that shaped the redesign.
Bounce Rate: ⬇️ 45 % points
Engagement: 2x brand site (5+ min)
Leads: ⬆️8.6%
Business lift: Case study helped push India scaling + Middle East expansion (10+ markets); core AR flow impacting 70k+ MAU across 10+ marquee clients.
Strategic: Reduced client churn risk, AR Module capability for future deployments.
Worked: Funnel differential diagnosis helped isolate scanning bleed; 3D immersive onboarding beat 2D (immersiveness-first for AR novices).
Key tactic: Non-leading user tests (contextual tasks + open debriefs) surfaced authentic pains like gesture mismatches and onboarding misses.
Growth: Prioritization by frequency/impact from 30+ tests; learned dynamic guidance for edge cases (poor lighting, bad spaces).
Repeat: Avoid 2D UI in immersive AR; build gesture flexibility from observed behaviors.

name: Visual Compare for Mass‑Market Buyers
summary: Led the end‑to‑end design and launch of a visual Compare module within 45 days, defining research, PRD, flows, and analytics while coordinating design, 3D, engineering, DevOps, and client teams.

blocks.text: Discover Compare empowers users to understand price differences with dual-view visuals, dynamic feature highlights, and detailed performance metrics - streamlining variant comparisons, clarifying value, and enabling confident decisions with speed and precision. All from a single platform.
Thus turning a markets text-only spec experience into a showroom-like visual comparison for mass-market car buyers and driving ~15% lead conversion from Compare sessions (vs ~5% industry benchmark).

items: Users: Mass-market buyers in India/Middle East comparing variants to understand "what do I get for extra money?"

Context: Discover suite (Landing → Configurator) lacked side-by-side visual comparison, missing the opportunity to build user confidence through showroom-like clarity with a compare tool; market offered textual tables.
Trigger: Major OEM needed full suite for new model launch (100k+ visitors expected during launch week, 30k+ per month for subsequent months).
Constraints: 45 days, small team, mobile+desktop+tablet, no-code toggle, no time slip.
Goal: Ship Compare in 45 days driving 30% engagement lift + ~4x industry benchmark lead conversion (achieved 3x).
North Star: Lead conversion from Compare. Primary: adoption, funnel progression.
Owned: Research, PRD, flows, analytics. Co-owned UX with Product Design and shipping with Delivery.
Stakeholders: 3D leads, EM, manager, Delivery Head, CTO/COO, client teams.
Approach: Research→insights→features→design→build→QA→integration.
Researched: Industry expert interviews + OEM/showroom insights + competitor audits confirmed visual gap.
Opportunity buckets: Visualization (mobile landscape), Knowledge (tables), Convenience (2-click switching), Leads.
Prioritized: Mobile+desktop [95%+ traffic], reused variant catalog UX, cut nice-to-haves (multi-state description tray).
Designed: Co-created Configurator→Compare→Lead flows and UX.
Coordinated: Aligned 3D (18 variant visuals), Engineering (module development), DevOps (anticipated scale), and client integration for launch day with Delivery.
Analytics: Designed events and dashboards to track adoption, engagement, and lead conversion.
~40% adoption from configurator users.
30% engagement lift over baseline.
~15% lead conversion from compare.
1.4x higher lead likelihood for Compare users.
Unlocked OEM expansion into 10+ Middle East markets on the back of a high-impact go-live 🚀
Constraints force impact/effort clarity
Prior research saves weeks
Reuse > reinvention under pressure
Orchestration = half the battle

name: 25% Faster Time-to-market
summary: Proactively stepped in to take end‑to‑end ownership of a critical 3D pipeline outside my formal remit that quietly powered and impacted almost every major initiative at the company.

blocks.text: Accelerated time-to-market by 25%, increased capacity to support ~1.5x parallel go-lives with cross-team collaboration by mapping 3D/tech pipeline bottlenecks, external benchmarking, process redesign.

blocks.caption: High-level handoff steps and optimization bucketing.

items: Hero: Sales team needed credible shorter go‑live promises to close deals faster without breaking delivery.
Bottleneck: 3D team capped at ~3–5 parallel go‑lives; 50+ day handoffs created fire‑drills during tight client timelines.
Pain: Previous optimization attempts failed; general belief that "this is just how 3D works," causing skepticism about change.
Stakes: product entering scaling phase; 3D capacity risked blocking major new deals.
Constraints: No hires, no SLA changes, <$1K research budget, 3–4 week timeline before Q2 deals.
My hypothesis: Manual work + outdated tools could yield 30–40% handoff reduction with targeted process/tooling fixes.
SMART objective: Cut 3D→Tech handoff from 50+ to ~<30days by Q2 end..
North Star: Average handoff duration (contract signed → tech-ready).
Primary KPIs: Handoff days, parallel go-lives capacity (target: 2x).
Secondary KPIs: 3D efficiency (fewer iterations/manual effort).
Owned: Discovery (shadowing/interviews), benchmarking (expert surveys), gap analysis, recommendations + sequencing with 3D/Graphics leads.
Process and frameworks: JTBD → Discovery/gap analysis → Solution Clustering → Prioritization → Improvement loop.
Key players: Manager/3D lead/Solutions lead; EM/CTO (approval).
Mapped 3D workflow: Shadowed artists, documented steps, tools, time per stage from intake to handoff.
Found hidden opportunities: Manual retopo, materials/textures, AO/light maps, file transfers that were normalized.
Benchmarked experts: Paid niche surveys + network revealed faster industry practices for retopo/maps.
Gap analysis: Identified 4 clusters - Retopo, maps, hardware, scripts - via internal vs external comparison.
Prioritized high-leverage: Chose retopo + maps + scripts for biggest time savings, lowest quality risk.
Tested retopo tools: Experimented, ran 3D team trials, selected best for our use case.
Fixed maps & scripts: Found faster AO/light map tools; defined Blender→internal pipeline scripts to cut iterations and manual redundant steps.
Drove adoption: Overcame "we've tried everything" skepticism with benchmarks + quick wins; iterated via 3D feedback.
Time-to-market: 25-30% faster
Capacity: ~1.5x parallel go-lives without hiring/outsourcing.
Sales impact: Enabled shorter go-live promises, strengthening deal differentiation.
Risk reduced: Fewer fire-drills on tight client timelines; more predictable delivery.
Better questions beat surface interviews: Shadowing revealed "normalized pain" being called "fine."
Evidence conquers skepticism: Benchmarks + quick experiments shifted "we've tried everything" mindset.
Gut + structure wins: Instinct + discovery framework overcame initial resistance.
Progress > perfection: 50+ → 35 days + 1.5x capacity proved scalable value despite not moonshot.
Loved proactive discovery: Expert conversations (internal/external) energized cross-team impact.
